screens.body:
A requirement is a clear statement of what the system must do, or what it must be like. It's a promise the finished software has to keep.

You already think this way. Ordering lunch: "chicken shawarma, no onion, under $25, here in 30 minutes." That's four requirements — specific, checkable, and exactly what a good software requirement looks like.

options: A clear, checkable statement of what the system must do or be like
A line of code
A guess about what users might want
check.question: A requirement is…

screens.heading: What a requirement is
screens.keyPoint: A promise the software must keep.

screens.body:
Functional requirements describe WHAT the system does: "users can post a task," "the app sends a confirmation email." They're the verbs — the features.

Non-functional requirements describe HOW WELL it does it: speed ("pages load in under 2 seconds"), security ("passwords are encrypted"), reliability, usability. They're the adverbs — the quality bar. Both kinds are requirements; only one of them is a feature.

options: Functional = what it does; non-functional = how well
Functional = fast; non-functional = slow
They're the same thing
check.question: Functional vs non-functional:

screens.heading: Two kinds of requirements
screens.keyPoint: Features are functional. Quality is non-functional.

screens.body:
Business requirements say WHY the organization wants the system: "reduce booking phone calls by half." User requirements say what USERS need to accomplish: "book a braid appointment in under 2 minutes."

Under those sit system requirements — the detailed, technical version developers actually build from. They stack: business goal → user need → system detail. If a system requirement doesn't trace back up to a real need, question it.

options: Business = why the org wants it; user = what users need to do
Business = code; user = design
User requirements don't matter
check.question: Business vs user requirements:

screens.heading: Levels of requirements
screens.keyPoint: Why → what users do → technical detail.

screens.body:
Elicitation is just a fancy word for drawing requirements OUT of people — because clients rarely hand you a neat list. The main techniques: interviews (ask directly), surveys (ask many), observation (watch them work), document review (read their forms and reports), workshops (get everyone in a room), and prototypes (show a mockup and ask "like this?").

No single technique catches everything. Interviews reveal opinions; observation reveals what people actually do — and those two often disagree.

options: Drawing requirements out using interviews, observation, surveys, and more
Writing code to guess requirements
Copying a competitor's features
check.question: Requirements elicitation means…

screens.heading: How you gather them
screens.keyPoint: Ask, watch, read, show — then combine.

screens.body:
The client interview is the highest-value technique, and it's a skill. Ask open questions ("walk me through your busiest day"), not yes/no ones. Listen more than you talk. Repeat back what you heard: "so the front desk handles payments — did I get that right?"

Watch for what they DON'T say, too. The receptionist who sighs every time the phone rings just told you something important about the current process — no words needed.

options: Open questions, active listening, confirming back
Yes/no questions as fast as possible
Telling the client what they need
check.question: A good client interview uses…

screens.heading: Interviewing like a pro
screens.keyPoint: Open questions. Listen hard. Confirm back.

screens.body:
A good requirement is clear, specific, and testable. "The system should be fast" fails all three — fast compared to what? Rewrite it: "search results appear within 2 seconds." Now you can actually test it.

Hunt down vague words: fast, user-friendly, some, many, usually, efficient. Each one is a future argument wearing a disguise. Replace every vague word with a number, a name, or a concrete behavior.

options: Clear, specific, and testable — vague words replaced with concrete detail
Long and impressive-sounding
As short as possible, details later
check.question: A good requirement is…

screens.heading: Writing requirements that work
screens.keyPoint: If you can't test it, it's not a requirement yet.

screens.body:
Raw interview notes become a numbered requirements list — each one short, each one testable. Then you prioritize, because no project gets everything: MUST have (launch without it and the system fails), SHOULD have (important but survivable), COULD have (nice polish for later).

Prioritizing is a conversation with the client, not a solo decision. Their "must" and your "must" might differ — and that's exactly the discussion that prevents building the wrong thing.

options: Numbered, testable items, prioritized must/should/could
One long paragraph describing everything
Whatever the developer feels like building
check.question: Interview notes become…

screens.heading: From conversation to checklist
screens.keyPoint: Number them, test them, prioritize them.

screens.body: IEEE (ieee.org) publishes the well-known standard for writing software requirements specifications — worth knowing it exists. AgileManifesto.org shows how agile teams capture requirements as user stories. OMG's UML pages (omg.org) cover how requirements get modeled once they're gathered.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: IEEE literally wrote the standard on requirements docs.
